articles.title: I believe I can take on any character: Bhagyashri Borse
articles.summary: Bhagyashri Borse’s recent choices have seen her explore contrasting characters — from a period role in Kaantha to a village girl in her latest release,
articles.body: Bhagyashri Borse’s recent choices have seen her explore contrasting characters — from a period role in Kaantha to a village girl in her latest release, Lenin. Continuing to explore diverse projects, she is currently shooting for Operation Ganga, an action thriller starring Mohanlal. Does she consciously seek out roles that allow her to explore different facets of her craft? She says she does, believing that an actor’s choices can help avoid being typecast.“Typecasting depends on how we choose our films and present ourselves,” she explains. “I’ve done a period film like Kaantha, I can be a cute village girl in Lenin, a serious doctor in Kingdom, or even a glamorous role. The audience is open and curious to see what you bring to the table. My aim is to explore a wide range of roles and continue growing as an actor. I’m not concerned about being typecast because I have confidence in my ability to tackle any character.”I want to keep exploring different kinds of roles and growing with each one. articles.summary: Ajay Devgn’s 'Drishyam 3: The Conclusion' has crossed the Rs 500 cr worldwide gross mark.
articles.body: Ajay Devgn’s 'Drishyam 3: The Conclusion' has crossed the Rs 500 cr worldwide gross mark. The film reached the milestone on its 12th day in theatres, earning Rs 8.50 cr net in India on Tuesday, October 13.According to Sacnilk, this marked a 41.7% increase over Monday’s Rs 6.00 cr. The latest domestic collection came from 14,846 shows. The film’s total India net collection has reached Rs 323.50 cr, while its domestic gross stands at Rs 387.80 cr. Overseas markets contributed Rs 2.50 cr on Day 12, taking the cumulative international gross to Rs 114.00 cr. articles.title: Kelly Clarkson 'has put us in danger,' Brooklyn store owner claims as bird's price tag soars to $15M
articles.summary: Adam Rubin claims Kelly Clarkson's viral dispute over a mechanical singing bird has led to threats and doxxing against his Brooklyn curiosity shop.
articles.body: Kelly Clarkson's public clash with a Brooklyn shop has left its owner concerned about more than a lost sale. Adam Rubin, co-owner of Art of Play and a children’s author, spoke with Fox News Digital inside the Brooklyn store Tuesday morning, claiming the singer has put his business in danger after their viral dispute over a $15,000 mechanical singing bird. The bird at the center of the controversy now has a staggering $15 million price tag. KELLY CLARKSON SLAMS BROOKLYN STORE OVER ‘PRETTY WOMAN’ TREATMENT "But I am afraid for the safety of our shop. Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger," Rubin told Fox News Digital. Rubin claimed the backlash has extended beyond angry comments online, with people associated with the business allegedly facing threats and having their personal information exposed. "We've got incredible support from our neighbors and fans over the past few days, and all of them have been attacked, threatened, doxed," he said. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS Rubin also accused Clarkson of an "abuse of power," arguing that the singer's enormous platform has intensified the backlash against his small business. Rubin argued that Clarkson's celebrity status carries a responsibility. "You can't just try to squash somebody like a bug and expect everybody to give you a pass," he said. Rubin also questioned why strangers would go to such lengths to attack a small business on behalf of a celebrity, expressing frustration that people who had never visited his store were joining the backlash. The mechanical bird that sparked the dispute has also undergone a dramatic price change. A photograph taken Tuesday by Fox News Digital shows a new sign beside Molly identifying the bird as a creation of artist Bliss Kolb, with an eye-popping price of $15 million. The sign describes Molly as "The world's most famous singing bird automata!" and lists its price as "$15,000,000." The new figure is 1,000 times the original $15,000 price at the center of Clarkson's complaint. Art of Play previously explained in a public statement that the original $15,000 figure referred to a nearly identical automaton available from artist Bliss Kolb, while Molly herself is permanently attached to the wall and serves as a fixture in the store's magic performances. PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE Rubin also addressed the dramatic price change during his conversation with Fox News Digital, pointing to the attention Molly has received since Clarkson's visit. He described the new figure as a matter of "supply and demand," while the store has maintained that the bird is not for sale. Rubin suggested Molly's sudden notoriety has made her one of the most recognizable mechanical birds in the world. The new sign offers a striking contrast to the original $15,000 price tag that Clarkson cited in her complaint. The price change adds another twist to a dispute that began Saturday when Clarkson visited the Brooklyn shop and later accused an employee of treating her as though she couldn't afford its merchandise. KELLY CLARKSON'S STORE CALLOUT SHOWS THE 'POWER' OF CELEBRITY STATEMENTS: EXPERT Clarkson initially took to social media to describe what she considered a humiliating shopping experience, comparing her treatment to Julia Roberts' character in the 1990 film "Pretty Woman." "Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me," Clarkson wrote. "Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale." The singer later doubled down on her account after Art of Play disputed her version of events. Clarkson maintained that she had pointed to a $15,000 price tag and was told the bird was available for purchase, but that an employee suggested finding her something comparable. "So you’re not only rude, you’re also a liar. Got it," Clarkson wrote in a follow-up post. Art of Play has maintained that the encounter was a misunderstanding. In its public response, the store explained that Molly is a permanent fixture in the shop and that employees had offered Clarkson the opportunity to purchase a similar bird from its creator. KELLY CLARKSON SAYS 'AMERICAN IDOL' PRODUCERS 'LIED' ABOUT $1M PRIZE The business also said another singing bird automaton, priced at approximately $2,000, was available. For Rubin, however, the controversy has become much more personal than a disagreement over an unusual piece of merchandise. During his conversation with Fox News Digital, the co-owner revealed that he had recently undergone a medical procedure and was not supposed to be working. "I'm not even supposed to be here today. I got a cancer removed from my face last week," Rubin said. "I'm getting the stitches out tonight." Rubin said his concern about the store's safety was the reason he came in despite recovering from the procedure. The co-owner also wanted to explain what Art of Play represents beyond the dispute that has suddenly brought it national attention. "This is a curiosity shop," Rubin told Fox News Digital. He described a business built around objects intended to inspire curiosity, including spinning tops, kaleidoscopes, puzzles, games and playing cards. "And the reason this place exists is to make people feel like a kid again," Rubin said. GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE The business began online before operating a small location in San Diego. Rubin said the Brooklyn shop opened approximately two years ago. Rubin, who is also a children's book author and magician, has spent years working in the world of illusion and performance. The Brooklyn store also houses a small theater that hosts close-up magic performances, with Molly serving as the opening act, according to Rubin. Art of Play has previously maintained that the bird is permanently attached to the wall and was not available for purchase. Despite the public dispute, Rubin said Clarkson would still be welcome back at the shop. "We messaged her. I don't know if she saw it. I don't know if she cares," Rubin said. Fox News Digital reached out to a representative for Clarkson for comment. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital's Janelle Ash and Christina Dugan-Ramirez contributed to this report.

articles.title: In 2021, Lee Marvin’s former 1936 Tucson estate sold for $1.825 million; after a meticulous restoration, the 7,261-square-foot home on 4.19 acres returned to the market with a $5.75 million asking price
articles.summary: In 2021, the former Tucson estate of Oscar-winning actor Lee Marvin sold for $1.825 million, ending decades of ownership by the actor’s family.
articles.body: In 2021, the former Tucson estate of Oscar-winning actor Lee Marvin sold for $1.825 million, ending decades of ownership by the actor’s family. After a meticulous restoration that preserved the home’s historic adobe character while adding contemporary comforts, the 7,261-square-foot property has returned to the market with an asking price of $5.75 million. Mansion Global reports that Marvin’s estate sold the residence to its current owners in 2021, and the new listing reflects both the scale of the renovation and the enduring appeal of architecturally significant desert homes.Located at 5055 North Calle La Vela in Tucson’s Catalina Foothills, the 1936 home was designed by celebrated architect Josias Joesler. It offers seven bedrooms, six and a half bathrooms, a guest house, pool, tennis court, and 4.19 acres of grounds, according to the active listing. The property is now positioned not merely as a luxury residence, but as a rare piece of Tucson’s architectural and Hollywood-linked history.A home with Hollywood historyLee Marvin purchased the estate in 1975 and lived there until his death in 1987. The actor, best known for winning the Academy Award for Best Actor for Cat Ballou in 1966, used the Tucson property as a private retreat away from the pressures of Hollywood. The house remained connected to Marvin’s family for many years after his death. It was finally sold by his estate in 2021 for $1.825 million, nearly 35 years after the actor’s passing, as per reports. That long ownership gives the home an unusually personal provenance, making it more than another high-end desert listing.Marvin was known for his rugged screen presence, but the Tucson estate reveals a quieter side of his life. Set among mature landscaping and open desert views, it offered the privacy and space that appealed to a major film star who valued time away from public attention.The Joesler adobe designThe residence was built in 1936 and designed by Swiss-born architect Josias Joesler, whose work helped define the look of Tucson’s early upscale residential developments. The estate is a classic example of Joesler mud-adobe construction, arranged around an expansive central courtyard with a large fountain.Its original character includes beamed ceilings, four fireplaces, mission-tile porches, chinked mortar, and scored concrete floors. These details give the home a warm, handcrafted quality that contrasts with the sleek finishes found in many newly built luxury properties.The layout connects indoor and outdoor living spaces through arched passageways, a design approach well suited to Tucson’s climate. Rather than treating the desert as something to shut out, the home opens toward patios, courtyards, and mountain views, creating a relaxed Southwestern atmosphere.A careful modern restorationThe current owners undertook a restoration intended to modernise the property without erasing its historic identity. The listing describes the home as fully revitalised, with its architectural integrity preserved and modern systems integrated throughout. The main house now includes a new chef’s kitchen that blends heritage detailing with high-performance appliances. Features include honed marble surfaces, custom cabinetry, a Wolf range, a Sub-Zero refrigerator, custom lighting, and new steel casement windows and doors that open to patios and broad views. This approach appears designed to appeal to today’s luxury buyers, who often want historic charm but expect contemporary kitchens, climate systems, lighting, and indoor-outdoor flow. The restoration therefore adds practical value while retaining the textures and proportions that make the original Joesler design distinctive, as per the reports.Space, grounds, and desert livingThe estate spans 7,261 square feet of living space and sits on 4.19 acres. Its seven bedrooms and six and a half bathrooms provide ample room for family, guests, staff, or a buyer who wants flexible space for work, entertainment, and recreation. Beyond the main residence, the property includes a guest house and a large bonus room with a bathroom. Outdoor amenities include a swimming pool and tennis court, making the estate suitable for both private relaxation and larger gatherings.The grounds are central to the home’s appeal. With mountain and sunset views, expansive outdoor areas, and a courtyard-centred plan, the estate offers the kind of secluded desert lifestyle that is difficult to recreate in a newer development.Why the price has risenThe jump from $1.825 million in 2021 to $5.75 million today is substantial, but the listing reflects more than market appreciation. The home has undergone a comprehensive restoration, and its combination of Joesler provenance, Lee Marvin history, acreage, and luxury amenities places it in a specialised segment of the Tucson market.Historic homes by recognised architects often attract buyers seeking originality, craftsmanship, and a sense of place. When those qualities are paired with celebrity history and extensive modern upgrades, the property becomes especially distinctive.At the same time, the asking price will depend on whether buyers see the restoration and provenance as worth the premium. The estate’s scale, location in Catalina Foothills, and rare surviving Joesler features give it a strong case, but its eventual sale price will show how the market values heritage-led luxury in Tucson.A rare desert legacyLee Marvin’s former Tucson estate is more than a restored celebrity home. It is a 1936 Joesler-designed adobe estate that has survived nearly a century while adapting to modern expectations.For buyers drawn to architecture, privacy, and history, the $5.75 million listing represents an opportunity to own a property with a genuine connection to one of Hollywood’s most memorable actors. For Tucson, it is also a reminder that the city’s older architectural landmarks can remain relevant when restoration respects their original character.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Sandown community hopes Town of Culture will bring change
articles.summary: Sandown was chosen in July as one of 15 finalists from nearly 400 hopefuls across the country.
articles.body:
Sandown on the Isle of Wight is in the final weeks of preparing its bid to become UK Town of Culture 2028.

The seaside resort was chosen in July as one of 15 finalists from nearly 400 hopefuls across the country vying for a £3m prize to stage a showcase of cultural events, with two runners-up each receiving £250,000.

Years of neglect have seen the once thriving tourist hotspot fall into disrepair, with the derelict hotels along the town's seafront becoming a constant target of vandalism .

But locals have told me that winning the Town of Culture competition is the catalyst for change that Sandown needs.

Ed Evans is a glass maker who runs the business his father set up in Sandown 30 years ago.

"Hopefully [winning] will encourage us to do some big public works around the town... that's what we've been asked to do, and I think the town definitely needs some brightening up, there's no doubt about that," he suggests.

"I always talk about the 'Sandown Smile'… on a Summer's day when you go down and everything's happening, it looks as good as any seaside town in the country.

"But then you get a sort of nasty, wet, windy, grey day in the Wintertime and no one's about and there's the tumbleweed blowing and you're looking around at some of the broken down hotels and stuff and you get a feeling that there's a bit of dereliction going on.

"We have potential and there is a lot of good things happening here and if we receive some funding we can show what we're doing here a bit more and just gild the edges.

"A lot of people complain about the town. We want to change that, we want to get rid of the bad spots and highlight the good stuff.

"I love the town, I love the beach particularly. I'm absolutely addicted to going down in the water, and [getting UK Town of Culture] would mean that I feel confident in the future of this place.

"I've never planned to move anywhere or change the premises of the business, and I like to think that we are moving into a better era, so I think it would give us confidence to keep going."

Lyssa Truman has lived in Sandown since she was eight, was made redundant after working for 33 years at the local leisure centre, and now runs exercise classes at The Fitness Hub at the town's old post office.

"I just think there are endless possibilities," she says about the bid.

"There are so many talented people in the area that could do with a break... and I just can see loads of little pop-up cafes, pop-up businesses, little markets where everyone would be able to come together, support each other, but also thrive and grow together as well, and I think that would really attract other people visiting here.

"The derelict buildings and the old hotels, things need to change there, and to just bring that High Street back as well because it was thriving years ago.

"All the different shops were open, and now some are a little run down, and there are lots of empty shops that actually just need to be brought back to life, to give people the opportunity without financially taking hold of them before they even get started.

"There are a lot of beautiful people here and it's not had that injection of money, and I don't think it will take much to make this place absolutely thrive.

"We've got the most beautiful bay in Sandown and when you look at that, you could be anywhere in the world, you really could, but imagine all these little extra things going on too, it'll just be incredible."

Vivette Fryatt, co-owner of the cafe Viv's Cooking, says Sandown remains "special" because of the people.

"I know there's a lot of room for improvement, but guess what? There's a lot also that's going on that's good," she says.

"[With prize money] visitors would see the beauty of Sandown, because in the Summertime they flock and they stay on the beachfront and even people on the island tell them that there's nothing in Sandown and that is so not true.

"Things are happening, things are here already. An injection of cash [could mean] fixing up the seafront, revitalising the High Street, and getting these shops open, even if it's to put community projects in that are attractive to visitors."

Ian Boyd works for environmental organisation The Common Space.

"Sandown sort of almost fizzled into existence in the middle of the 19th century," he explains.

"It evolved overnight as a place for people to come and stay in this beautiful setting and that kind of Victorian idea of tourism has never left, and so the High Street and the seafront were all designed around that model.

"But everything has changed and so Sandown needs to change. A consequence of that is it's struggled and it's had hard times.

"It's perhaps the one place on the island that can genuinely change trajectory... it captures so much of the island spirit, it's a beautiful seafront environment, it's bookended by nationally important landscapes, it's set within a Unesco World Biosphere , it has all of these gifts.

"It has a strong cultural story, it has an amazing diversity of landscapes, seascapes, streetscapes, but it's young enough to change direction, to take a new route, and I think that's what Town of Culture will do for us."

The bid team is putting together a six-month programme of events culminating in the Tide Turner Festival, a major celebration of arts and science.

It would tell Sandown's story over 100 million years from the footprints of the dinosaurs, via Charles Darwin's momentous On the Origin of Species - which he began working on in the town - to the present-day manufacture of pioneering vertipools that provide artificial marine habitats for a changing planet.

The town will find out if it has made it through to the next round of the competition in November.

The overall winner will be announced next year.

These interviews have been edited for length and clarity.

articles.title: ‘We had 15-20 versions of the ending’: ‘Drishyam 3’ co-writer Aamil Keeyan Khan reveals they wrote 100 drafts for some scenes, debated Ajay Devgn’s darker side and reworked the climax to surprise audiences
articles.summary: ‘Drishyam 3: The Conclusion’ has crossed the Rs 500 crore mark worldwide, adding to the success of the Hindi thriller starring Ajay Devgn, Tabu and
articles.body: ‘Drishyam 3: The Conclusion’ has crossed the Rs 500 crore mark worldwide, adding to the success of the Hindi thriller starring Ajay Devgn, Tabu and Jaideep Ahlawat. In a recent interview, co-writer Aamil Keeyan Khan revealed that the writing team developed 15-20 versions of the ending and rewrote several portions of the screenplay to keep audiences guessing. He also opened up about Akshaye Khanna’s exit shortly before filming, the challenges of introducing Ahlawat’s character and the debate over how dark Vijay Salgaonkar could become.Aamil Keeyan Khan on rewriting ‘Drishyam 3’ with '15-20 versions of the ending’The success of ‘Drishyam 3: The Conclusion’ reflects the risks taken by director Abhishek Pathak and his writing team. Unlike the first two Hindi instalments, which were based on the Malayalam franchise, the third film follows an original story developed for the Hindi adaptation.Speaking to Mid-Day, Aamil Keeyan Khan, who co-wrote the screenplay and penned the dialogues, credited Pathak’s vision and Ajay Devgn’s support for helping the team bring the story to the screen.“Ajay Sir stood behind us like a rock, supporting us in whatever we did. We narrated the first draft to him in April 2025, he loved it. After that, we made a lot of revisions and he was on board with everything,” Khan recalled.The writers faced the challenge of concluding the story of Vijay Salgaonkar and his family, who covered up an accidental murder in the first film. With audiences already familiar with the franchise’s twists and turns, the team had to find a way to deliver a fresh and unpredictable conclusion.Khan revealed that the ending went through numerous iterations as the writers attempted to stay ahead of audience expectations.“We had to set Jaideep sir’s character dynamics with other players, and we had to deliver in seven days! We wrote 100 drafts for some scenes. We even had 15-20 versions of the ending. It was a humongous challenge as people had seen the first two parts and we had to surprise them. A lot of [the script] was scrapped and rewritten in those seven days,” he said.Akshaye Khanna’s exit created a seven-day writing challengeThe film’s development faced another major hurdle when Akshaye Khanna exited the project a week before filming began. The team had to rework the screenplay and establish new character dynamics after Jaideep Ahlawat came on board.According to Khan, introducing Ahlawat’s character required substantial changes to the script, with the writers working against a tight deadline.The team rewrote portions of the story in just seven days, revisiting scenes and exploring different possibilities to ensure the new character fitted into the existing narrative. Khan’s account highlights the scale of the last-minute adjustments required to keep the production moving without compromising the suspense at the heart of the franchise.The extensive rewriting also reflected the challenge of creating an original Hindi storyline while meeting audience expectations for a franchise known for its carefully constructed reveals.‘Is that really Vijay?’: The writers debated how dark Ajay Devgn’s character could becomeBeyond the ending and the changes to the screenplay, one question continued to shape the story: how far would Vijay Salgaonkar go to protect his family?Khan explained that the writers explored several versions in which Vijay became considerably darker before reconsidering whether those choices remained true to the character audiences had followed across the franchise.“Vijay is doing the wrong thing for the right cause. There were so many drafts where he has gone much darker and then we pulled ourselves back, thinking, ‘Is that really Vijay?’ We toyed with the idea of him going completely dark.”The moral conflict at the centre of Vijay’s character has been a defining element of the ‘Drishyam’ films. While his actions are driven by his determination to protect his family, the consequences of those decisions have repeatedly placed him in ethically complicated situations.For the third instalment, the writers had to balance that established characterisation with the need to raise the stakes and deliver an ending audiences would not easily anticipate.‘Drishyam 3: The Conclusion’ box office collectionThe film’s commercial performance has added another milestone to the franchise. By Day 12, ‘Drishyam 3: The Conclusion's total domestic net collection is Rs 323.50 crore and India gross collection is Rs 387.80 crore. Overseas, the film's worldwide overseas gross collection stands at Rs. 501.80 crore.Directed by Abhishek Pathak, ‘Drishyam 3: The Conclusion’ stars Ajay Devgn, Tabu and Jaideep Ahlawat, alongside Shriya Saran, Ishita Dutta and other cast members. articles.title: Vishal Bhardwaj: Gaana Rekha ko hota hai aur gaa main raha hoon
articles.summary: This week, Vishal Bhardwaj was expected to perform at Safdarjung Tomb, but security restrictions in central Delhi necessitated a change of venue.
articles.body: This week, Vishal Bhardwaj was expected to perform at Safdarjung Tomb, but security restrictions in central Delhi necessitated a change of venue. Instead, he performed at a baithak for a small gathering, sharing an evening of conversations and songs. “Last moment pe kisi wajah se hamara venue change hua aur hum yahan pe mil rahe hain. Mujhe lagta hai jo hota hai achhe ke liye hi hota hai ki hum yahan mil rahe hain. Yahan intimacy aur zyada lag rahi hai. Ghazalein aur baatein,” he told the gathering.It was an evening that offered a glimpse of Vishal Bhardwaj the director, screenwriter, lyricist, poet and composer, but foremost, the singer. Seated across from him in the front row, Rekha Bhardwaj listened to his songs from the audience.Mujhe aisa mauka kabhi kabhi milta hai jab main gaa raha hoon aur Rekha sunein: Vishal BhardwajThree years ago, Vishal and Rekha Bhardwaj performed live together for a Delhi audience for the first time. Back then, they spoke of how sharing the stage had been a dream for years. Since then, the two have performed together in Delhi a couple of times. However, this evening at Ibtida-Ek Mehfil belonged to Vishal Bhardwaj, the singer. The stories he narrated drew from his many worlds, while an attentive audience listened, hanging on to his every word.He began the evening with the ghazal “Jaana tumko jaana ho toh mat aana” from Khufiya (2023) and said, “Rekha sang this ghazal. I'm very happy that Rekha is late. She is going to be sitting in the audience today. Mujhe bhi aisa mauka kabhi kabhi milta hai jab main gaa raha hoon aur woh sunein. Usually, ulta hi hota hai. Obviously, hona bhi chahiye. Rekha bahut hi zyada achhi singer hai. Main uske aas-paas bhi nahi hoon. Par ab Rekha nahi hai toh aur bhi mauka banta hai sunane ka.”Sharing a joke, he said, “Gaana Rekha ko hota hai aur gaa main raha hoon.” Later in the evening, when he invited Rekha Bhardwaj on stage, she told the audience that Vishal had been doing more riyaaz than her these days. Vishal added, “Rekha meri guru hai.”Waise maine Meerut se schooling ki, main apne aap ko Dilli se zyada maanta hoon. Mujhe lagta hai main zinda hua ya artiste bana, woh main Dilli ki badaulatMain apne aap ko Dilli ka bashinda maanta hoon: Vishal BhardwajBhardwaj is an alumnus of Hindu College. Whenever he performs in Delhi, he invites his friends to the evening and introduces them to the audience.“Main apne aap ko Dilli se zyada maanta hoon. Waise maine Meerut se schooling ki. Mujhe lagta hai main zinda hua ya artiste bana, woh main Dilli ki badaulat. Main Dilli ke college mein padhne aaya tha Meerut se,” he shared, adding, “Composer toh tha main lekin iss profession mein aane ka mera bilkul bhi iraada nahi tha. Cricketer banna chahta tha, isliye main Delhi University mein aaya tha. Main kharab student tha bahut. Jo admission bhi hua tha, woh sports quota mein hua tha. Isliye Dilli se mera bahut hi alag rishta hai. Main apne aap ko Dilli ka bashinda maanta hoon. Uss daur mein mehfilon ka concept bahut hua karta tha, ki uss waqt ke jo bade-bade artistes hain, woh gaddon mein baith ke gaaya karte thay saath mein. Gaane mein aur sunne waale mein faasla hota gaya. Aur hum log uss cheez ko bhool gaye.”Talking about the concept of a baithak, he said, “Jab audience ko achha lag raha hai toh pata chalta hai, jab achha nahi lagta hai toh pata chal jata hai, toh ye bahut khoobsurat hai.”‘Pata nahi aakhiri baar mohabbat hoti hai ya nahi. Pehli baar toh zaroor hoti hai’Bhardwaj would often stop singing to explain the nuances of the words and the origins of a song. Before singing Pehli baar mohabbat ki hai from Kaminey, he said, “Gulzar sahab ne separation sun ke ye line di thi - pehli baar mohabbat ki hai, aakhri baar mohabbat ki hai. Bahut hi khoobsurat line hai. Waise pata nahi aakhri baar mohabbat hoti hai ya nahi. Pehli baar toh zaroor hoti hai.”He recalled that after recording the song Raat ke dhaai baje, he felt its soul was demanding something else. He then recorded another version of the song.Before performing Paani Paani Re from Maachis, he recalled his lifelong friendship with Lata Mangeshkar, who had asked him to treat her like any new singer, not the legendary artiste she was. He remembered her sincerity, grace and humility.'Pyaar mein itni bhi khamoshi theek nahi, gussa ho toh emoji mein bolo na'Two poets who have left a deep impression on the country, Bashir Badr and Gulzar, kept coming up in Bhardwaj’s anecdotes. Both are immensely close to him, he said and shared, “Bashir Badr sahab mere ustad rahe hain aur woh kehte thay ki ghazal jo hoti hai woh contemporary hoti chali jaati hai aur uska maza bhi tabhi hota hai jab rozmarra ki jo bhasha hai woh usmein use ho. Uska connection tab banta hai. Koshish ye hai ki rozmarra ki baatein ismein ho.”He then sang songs that had references to live location, Gmail and Google Maps. As always, he left the gathering in awe when he sang, “Pyaar mein itni bhi khamoshi theek nahi, gussa ho toh emoji mein bolo na.”'Mujhe toh lag raha tha maine aap logon ko phansa ke rakha hai'Bhardwaj had prepared some new sher by the poet Farhat Ehsas for the audience. Toh woh tha — ‘Ilaaj apna karate fir rahe ho jaane kis-kis se. Mohabbat karke dekho na, mohabbat kyun nahi karte?’”The audience applauded. Bhardwaj said that he bought the poet’s book afterwards. Towards the end of the evening, he sang two or three ghazals based on his own shers that he had not performed before.“We (all the musicians with me on stage) have been singing all these film songs and looking at each other again and again, thinking that we didn't sing those that we had been preparing,” he said.When he ended the evening on a high note with Chappa Chappa Charkha Chale, requests written on tiny chits began arriving one after another. articles.title: Priyadarshan thinks 'Hera Pheri 3' starring Akshay Kumar, Paresh Rawal, Suniel Shetty might never get made: 'Too many complications, I'd need chapters and chapters to talk about it'
articles.summary: The future of ‘Hera Pheri 3’ continues to look uncertain, with the much-awaited sequel facing a series of setbacks, including Paresh Rawal’s exit and
articles.body: The future of ‘Hera Pheri 3’ continues to look uncertain, with the much-awaited sequel facing a series of setbacks, including Paresh Rawal’s exit and return, a legal dispute over the franchise’s rights and Priyadarshan’s decision to step away from the project. The filmmaker, who directed the original 2000 comedy, has now expressed doubts about whether the third instalment will ever be made.Priyadarshan opened up about the complications surrounding ‘Hera Pheri 3’ and also revealed why he declined Akshay Kumar’s offer to direct ‘Bhagam Bhag 2’. The filmmaker explained that he is reluctant to revisit successful films unless there is a compelling story that can surpass the original.When asked why he decided to distance himself from ‘Hera Pheri 3’, Priyadarshan pointed to the multiple issues surrounding the film.“That has a lot of other complications, too many complications. I’d need chapters and chapters to talk about it,” he said in an interview with Hindustan Times.Asked if he thought the sequel would eventually make it to theatres, the director gave a blunt response: “I don’t think it will ever get made”.Priyadarshan also explained why he chose not to direct ‘Bhagam Bhag 2’, despite Akshay Kumar approaching him for the project. According to the filmmaker, a sequel should only be made if its story is stronger than that of the original film.He said, “That is why I never do sequels because the reason that you are doing part 2, it should be better than the part one, like with the Terminator franchise where part 2 was a better film than part 1. Unless you have a much better story, you shouldn’t do it. People always make a sequel when the first one really works, so if you don’t better it, there is no value for the franchise.”The director further argued that sequels often capitalise on the goodwill of the original rather than bringing a fresh creative vision to the screen.“What happens with sequels is that they are selling the value of the first film. They are not making a film, they are making a project, and I am not interested in projects. Even with Bhagam Bhaag, Akshay asked me ‘are you interested in directing?’ I said no. The question is that when you make a film and people appreciate it, why do you want to go and spoil that appreciation by doing a part 2. That’s why I refuse directing sequels. Let other people make sequels of my films, I am fine with that.”Priyadarshan had confirmed in July that he was no longer associated with ‘Hera Pheri 3’. This came after he had earlier expressed optimism about the project moving forward. At the time, he told Hindustan Times, “I am not associated with Hera Pheri 3 at the present. To the best of my knowledge, Hera Pheri 3 will never hit the screens due to lots of legal issues and personal conflicts. Whether I am involved or not is unimportant,”The filmmaker has also spoken about his troubled equation with producer Firoz Nadiadwala. In an interview with Mid-Day, Priyadarshan alleged that the producer had insulted him on several occasions, including making disparaging remarks about his version of the original ‘Hera Pheri’.“Firoz told Akshay, ‘You have the rights to make Hera Pheri 3, but never make it with Priyadarshan. That’s my only request.’ He has insulted me so many times. He told me that my cut of Hera Pheri (2000) looked like a poor man’s version and that he had to edit my five-hour movie,” the director said.Priyadarshan also revealed that he had initially agreed to return for the third film because he saw the potential for it to become one of the country’s biggest franchises. He said Akshay Kumar, Suniel Shetty and Paresh Rawal had personally requested him to direct the sequel and were enthusiastic about the story he narrated to them.“I initially agreed to do the third part with Akshay because I thought I could make one of this country’s biggest franchises. If I had directed it, I could’ve made it bigger than Dhurandhar. Akshay, Suniel and Paresh requested me to make Hera Pheri 3. When I narrated the story to them, they were all excited,” he added.The sequel has faced several hurdles beyond the director’s departure. Last year, Paresh Rawal unexpectedly exited the project, prompting Akshay Kumar to file a lawsuit seeking Rs 25 crore from the actor. Rawal later confirmed that the differences had been resolved amicably and that he would return to the film.The franchise also stars Suniel Shetty, who played Shyam in the earlier films, alongside Akshay as Raju and Paresh as the much-loved Baburao Ganpatrao Apte. Despite the enduring popularity of the comedy series, the latest developments have left the fate of ‘Hera Pheri 3’ uncertain.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Russell Brand Was ‘Ruthless and Calculated’ With a ‘Voracious’ Desire for ‘Sexual Contact,’ Prosecution Alleges in Rape Trial Opening Statement
articles.summary: Russell Brand was “ruthless and calculated” with an “indiscriminate and voracious” desire for sexual contact, the prosecution alleged in its opening statemen...
articles.body:
Russell Brand was "ruthless and calculated" with an "indiscriminate and voracious" desire for sexual contact, the prosecution alleged in its opening statement at the actor and comedian's rape trial in London.

Brand has been charged with three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault. He has pleaded not guilty and denied all charges.

Arriving to Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday morning, Brand sported a black suit, pinstriped shirt, loose white tie and sunglasses. He was accompanied by his wife, Laura Gallacher, whose hand he clasped. According to BBC News , Brand told reporters on his way inside: "I feel blessed. I feel of course concerned, but hopeful that this process will lead to good outcomes for everybody — that is my prayer," he said. Inside the courtroom, Brand appeared to be rubbing what looked like a rock or pebble in his hand.

Riel Karmy-Jones KC is leading the prosecution and set out the case against Brand. As the BBC reports, the six alleged victims "did not know each other, have never met each other" and "came forward independently of each other," Karmy-Jones noted.

Brand was "ruthless and calculated" and "sometimes might tell women what they wanted to hear" to satisfy his sexual appetite, Karmy-Jones alleged. "The circumstances of the offending were as wide and as varied as the defendant's career," she said. "His strong desire for some form of sexual contact was indiscriminate and voracious."

Karmy-Jones called Brand "a flirt with a huge sexual appetite — childlike in his expectation that his every desire should be met."

The jury was selected on Tuesday, consisting of eight men and four women. The case involves six female plaintiffs, all of whom are given automatic lifelong anonymity according to U.K. law, and relates to alleged offenses that occurred between 1999 and 2009.

In the mid-2000s, Brand was best known as a comedian and actor, presenting shows such as "Big Brother's Big Mouth" and starring in films such as "Get Him to the Greek" and "Forgetting Sarah Marshall." He has since pivoted to podcasting and influencing online.

The trial is expected to run for six weeks.

articles.title: Dani García, chef: "La sopa de ajo más rica no lleva chorizo, el truco es tostar el pan y añadir una cucharada de pimentón"
articles.standfirst: El cocinero malagueño comparte su receta de sopa castellana, un plato tradicional de cuchara ideal para los días fríos
articles.summary: El cocinero malagueño comparte su receta de sopa castellana, un plato tradicional de cuchara ideal para los días fríos
articles.body: Con la llegada del frío, los platos de cuchara vuelven a ganar protagonismo en las cocinas. Las sopas calientes son una de las opciones más sencillas para entrar en calor sin gastar demasiado, especialmente cuando se preparan con ingredientes tan básicos como el pan, el ajo, el aceite de oliva y el caldo. Sin embargo, hay pequeños detalles que pueden marcar la diferencia en el resultado final. El chef Dani García compartió en el programa de TVE 'Hacer de comer' su versión de la sopa castellana, también conocida como sopa de ajo, con varios consejos para potenciar su sabor. Entre ellos, destaca tostar el pan antes de incorporarlo a la cazuela y enriquecer el caldo con un hueso de jamón. El cocinero malagueño, que cuenta con tres estrellas Michelin a lo largo de su trayectoria, apuesta por una preparación tradicional con algunos detalles que ayudan a conseguir una sopa más sabrosa y con una textura agradable. La receta incluye pan, ajo, caldo de ave, pimentón dulce, huevos y jamón ibérico, ingredientes habituales en este plato de la gastronomía española. Uno de los pasos que el chef considera importantes es tostar las rebanadas de pan antes de añadirlas al caldo. No se trata únicamente de calentarlas: el objetivo es que adquieran un ligero tostado que aporte más sabor y ayude a conservar parte de su textura durante la cocción. Dani García recomienda frotar después el pan caliente con un diente de ajo para intensificar su aroma. En la receta que preparó para TVE, utiliza entre seis y ocho rodajas de pan, preferiblemente de una hogaza, que después incorpora a la cazuela con el resto de los ingredientes. El cocinero explicó que el tostado aporta un matiz diferente al resultado final y permite que el pan se integre en el caldo sin deshacerse por completo. La idea es conseguir una sopa con cuerpo, pero sin que todos los ingredientes terminen convertidos en una masa uniforme. Otro de sus consejos tiene que ver con el caldo. Aunque se puede utilizar uno envasado, García propone añadir un hueso de jamón y dejarlo cocer entre una hora y media y dos horas para que el líquido gane sabor. De esta forma, se puede enriquecer una base preparada sin necesidad de elaborar un caldo desde cero. El pimentón es otro de los ingredientes fundamentales de esta receta, pero conviene prestar atención al momento de incorporarlo. Si se quema, puede aportar un sabor amargo que perjudique el resultado final. La recomendación es añadirlo cuando los ajos comiencen a cocinarse en el aceite, controlando la temperatura y removiendo brevemente antes de incorporar el pan y el caldo. El chef utiliza una cucharada de pimentón dulce para preparar su versión de la sopa castellana. Una vez incorporados los ingredientes, la sopa debe cocer durante unos 20 minutos para que el pan absorba el líquido y los sabores se integren. Después llega el turno de los huevos, que se añaden con el fuego bajo para que se cocinen suavemente. García prefiere que la clara quede cuajada, pero que la yema conserve una textura líquida. Para evitar que algún huevo esté en mal estado, recomienda cascarlo primero en un recipiente aparte antes de incorporarlo a la cazuela.

articles.title: Inside Imran Khan's Karjat home which is a lavish vacation villa that he designed himself with 3D modelling, spent a year observing the property's sunlight, landscape, seasonal changes
articles.summary: Imran Khan’s home in Karjat offers a refreshing departure from the usual idea of a luxury holiday property.
articles.body: Imran Khan’s home in Karjat offers a refreshing departure from the usual idea of a luxury holiday property. Surrounded by trees and hills, the house has been designed to blend into its natural surroundings, with expansive windows, open interiors and understated finishes. The actor took on the design himself, teaching himself 3D modelling and spending a year observing the property’s sunlight, landscape and seasonal changes before settling on the final plan.In 2024, Imran gave followers a glimpse of the home through a series of photographs, revealing a property shaped by careful planning rather than conventional luxury.The pictures show airy rooms with sloping ceilings, exposed wooden beams and floor-to-ceiling glass doors that open out towards the greenery. One space features a large window overlooking the trees, while another connects directly to a wooden deck through sliding glass doors. The bedroom follows the same understated aesthetic, with broad windows bringing in natural light, a built-in wooden unit along one wall, a simple bed and a lounge chair. The interiors have been kept uncluttered, allowing the architecture and views to take centre stage.The house stands on a sloping piece of land, with its raised structure designed around the natural contours of the site. Brick walls, a stone base and a pitched roof give the building a simple, earthy character. Rather than transforming the terrain, the design makes room for the trees, open spaces and other features of the landscape.When he shared the photographs in 2024, Imran revealed that he had designed the house despite having no formal architectural training. His interest in learning new skills led him to teach himself 3D modelling, while his approach to the project involved spending considerable time understanding the property before construction began.“So… one of the things I did over the past few years was to build a house. While I’ve played an architect in a few films, I can’t actually pretend to have any kind of training or expertise… but I do enjoy tinkering and learning stuff!” he wrote.The land came with its own challenges, including uneven terrain, seasonal streams and a nearby cliff. Instead of altering these features to accommodate a conventional villa, Imran wanted the house to respond to its surroundings.“The intention was not to build a lavish vacation villa, rather to make something that takes it cues from the landscape. The house isn’t meant to be the view, it’s a shelter from which to admire the view.”He also described how he familiarised himself with the site before deciding on the design, observing how the landscape changed throughout the year.“I spent the first year going to the site at various times to watch the sunrise and sunset, the flow of the streams when it rains, and the changing foliage through the seasons.”In a 2024 conversation with comedians Sapan Varma, Raunaq Rajani and Prashasti Singh, Imran spoke in greater detail about the process, explaining how he learnt to use 3D modelling software and developed the design himself rather than hiring an architect.“So, I designed, and have just completed building a house out in Karjat. I work without an architect. I taught myself 3D modelling, I got the software and designed the thing. I spent a year going to the property, after we’d purchased it, to track the movement of the sun. Different times of day, different times of year. I spent one year, 2021, tracking the movement of the sun, to see how the light would be. I worked with a contractor and a structural engineer, but the design and the 3D model I built.”The actor also opted for construction techniques inspired by homes in the surrounding villages. Instead of a conventional concrete slab, the house was built using a stone base, single-storey brick walls, steel roof beams and insulated roofing sheets, with a contractor and structural engineer helping bring his design to life.The construction photographs show the exposed beams and sloping roof taking shape, elements that remain central to the finished home. Inside, the large windows and glass doors create a seamless connection between the living spaces and the outdoors, making the surrounding greenery an integral part of the design.For Imran, the process was as much about understanding the land as it was about building a house. He acknowledged that the project took time, but said the effort paid off. He also noted that designing and building the property himself worked out to be less expensive than purchasing one of the ready-made villas being advertised in the area.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Racial bias in London music event licensing, report says
articles.summary: Genres including Afrobeats, hip-hop and R&B are routinely flagged as "high risk", a report finds.
articles.body:
Black-led music events in London face disproportionate restrictions and cancellations because of "racial bias" in licensing and policing, a report has concluded.

The Race Equality in Music Event Licensing (REMEL) report , commissioned by the Greater London Authority, said that black-led events were blocked at higher rates than white-led events in the capital, and South Asian-led events also faced restrictions.

The report said genres including Afrobeats, hip-hop, drill, R&B and dancehall were routinely flagged as "high risk", while indie, pop and rock nights faced less scrutiny.

Cameron Leslie, chairman of the mayor's London Nightlife Taskforce, welcomed the report and its recommendations.

The Metropolitan Police said it understood the "concerns and differing views" on the matter, and would "carefully consider the report's findings".

London Councils, which represents local authorities across London, has been asked for comment.

The report, carried out by Black Lives in Music, was informed by interviews, focus groups, workshops, a survey and internet research. Freedom of Information (FOI) requests were also submitted but were largely rejected or only partially answered.

Researchers said that a lack of race-disaggregated licensing data (data broken down into racial and ethnic categories), limited official datasets and rejected FOIs made some patterns difficult to measure.

Alongside black-led events, the report also looked at South Asian-led events, but found that South Asian music was "largely invisible within licensing records".

The report suggested that South Asian music and cultural events were often allowed to proceed through "negotiation, modified hours and conditions", but said the evidence did not demonstrate that South Asian music was "disproportionately cancelled" in the capital, and incomplete licensing records made firm conclusions difficult.

The report was welcomed by the Musicians' Union, UK Music, the Music Venue Trust, the Night Time Industries Association and LIVE trust, among other organisations.

Dr Hakeem Stevens, report co-author and lead researcher, said they looked back to the beginning of recorded sound in the late 1800s as part of the research.

"We've got incidents of licensing decision issues based around race going back that far - to the 1910s, 1900s and so forth," he said.

"People assume that the problems came about in the last 10 to 15 years," he said, adding that the issue dated back to approximately 100 years.

Issues dating back more than a century were not cited within the report, but the legacy of Form 696 was discussed.

The Metropolitan Police form, which was scrapped in 2017, had been dubbed a "racist" risk assessment.

It was introduced in 2005 after a spate of shootings at London club nights, and influenced similar forms used by other police forces in England .

The report said that licensing decisions for live music events were influenced by risk and "racialised assumptions about culture and safety".

The report said this meant that "institutional racism" was "reproduced" through routine processes rather than explicit bans or policies.

Event organisers and venue owners told researchers that "police intelligence" was "routinely used to justify heightened scrutiny of black and South Asian events", and gave examples of being asked to fund a police presence or private security for an event.

One licensing officer interviewed for the report said that sometimes this intelligence was credible, and other times it was "hearsay".

"These practices act as a hidden form of economic exclusion," the report said.

"Events are not directly banned but are made logistically or financially impossible to run.

"Police intelligence, which is often unverified, becomes a tool for discouraging organisers and forcing them to pay additional costs."

The report added: "Each [event] cancellation represents not only a financial loss but also a denial of economic and cultural participation in one of the UK's most successful creative industries."

Charisse Beaumont, chief executive of Black Lives in Music, said entrepreneurs and artists in the capital at the beginning of their careers were "oppressed and suppressed due to the licensing system" and its "disparities".

Kwame Otiende, owner of The Jago, a live music venue in Dalston, and chairman of Hackney Council's Licensing Committee, said: "The report evidences what we have always known. Inequality has always existed, especially within the night-time economy."

The report set out 19 recommendations, including a review of the licensing system, transparent evidence standards and a requirement for cultural impact assessments for major licensing decisions.

It also called for "a licensing system rooted in fairness, transparency and equality", adding: "Safety must never be used as a cover for racial bias, cultural misunderstanding or disproportionate restriction."

Michael Kill, chief executive of the Night Time Industries Association, said the report highlighted an "uncomfortable reality" in parts of the licensing, policing and local authority decision-making system, and provided "evidence, recommendations and a platform for change".

Metropolitan Police commander Neerav Patel said the force understood the "concerns and differing views" on the matter.

"Our focus will remain on making fair, evidence-based contributions to the licensing process which balance the interests of venues, promoters, artists and local communities, while never compromising on our ultimate priority which is to keep Londoners safe," he said.

"We will carefully consider the report's findings in that context."

articles.title: Kangana Ranaut's ‘Queen Forever’ gets a breather as Bombay High Court refuses to stay sequel amid Phantom Studios’ intellectual property dispute
articles.summary: The Bombay High Court has refused to stay the production and release of Queen Forever, the upcoming sequel to Kangana Ranaut’s 2014 hit Queen.
articles.body: The Bombay High Court has refused to stay the production and release of Queen Forever, the upcoming sequel to Kangana Ranaut’s 2014 hit Queen. On Wednesday, Justice Sandeep Marne declined interim relief sought by Phantom Studios India Pvt Ltd in its legal dispute with Jiostar India Pvt Ltd, allowing work on the film to continue for now.Bombay High Court declines interim injunctionAccording to a Hindustan Times report, a single-judge bench led by Justice Sandeep Marne rejected Phantom Studios’ plea for a temporary injunction against Jiostar, which is producing Queen Forever. Phantom Studios, a co-producer of the original film, argued that Queen had earned critical acclaim, performed well commercially and built considerable goodwill over the years.The studio also pointed out that the proposed sequel features Kangana Ranaut, who headlined the original film. Phantom Studios has challenged the project on the grounds that it cannot proceed without its consent.Phantom Studios claims equal ownership of ‘Queen’ intellectual propertyIn its lawsuit, Phantom Studios maintained that it and Jiostar jointly own equal, 50 per cent shares in the intellectual property rights associated with Queen. The studio cited their co-production agreement, arguing that the contract grants both parties equal rights over derivative works based on the film.These rights, according to Phantom Studios, extend to sequels, prequels, remakes and other adaptations involving the original film’s story, characters or underlying material. The studio contended that developing Queen Forever without its approval would violate the terms of the agreement.Studio says it sent multiple notices to Jiostar since April 2026Phantom Studios claimed that it had never given its consent for a sequel, remake, adaptation or any other derivative work based on Queen. It further stated that it had sent multiple caution notices to Jiostar since April 2026, asking the company to halt plans for a sequel or any project associated with the original film.According to the studio, Jiostar did not provide details of the proposed project despite these communications. Phantom Studios subsequently approached the High Court, seeking urgent intervention to prevent the film from progressing without its written approval.What Phantom Studios wanted the court to restrainEmphasising the urgency of the matter, Phantom Studios argued that the film was reportedly scheduled for release in the coming months. It sought an order restraining Jiostar, the producer and their representatives from making, developing, producing, shooting, completing, releasing, distributing, broadcasting, streaming, marketing, promoting, advertising or otherwise exploiting a sequel, prequel, remake, adaptation or derivative work under the titles Queen Forever or Queen 2 without its prior written consent.However, the High Court declined to grant the requested interim injunction at this stage.More about 'Queen Forever''Queen Forever' is the upcoming official sequel to the critically acclaimed 2014 comedy-drama 'Queen', starring Kangana Ranaut as she reprises her iconic role as Rani Mehra. The film reunites Kangana with director Vikas Bahl.Disclaimer: The information in this report is based on a legal hearing as reported by a third-party source. The details provided represent allegations made by the parties involved and are not proven facts. articles.title: Newly released surveillance video shows Kelly Clarkson in Brooklyn store
articles.summary: Clarkson ignited a dispute with a New York novelty store over the weekend.
articles.body:
New surveillance video is shedding light about the circumstances behind the viral feud between singer Kelly Clarkson and a novelty store in Brooklyn.

The video, which was obtained by the "Pablo Torre Finds Out" podcast and does not have any audio, appears to show the moments leading up to Clarkson's social media complaint about the customer service treatment she received at Art of Play, a magic and games store.

Clarkson appears in the grainy surveillance video wearing a yellow hoodie and baseball cap. She can be seen browsing items in the store, testing a kaleidoscope and examining a wooden songbird on display named "Molly."

The singer is then seen waving at an employee about the bird, setting the kaleidoscope down and moving toward the exit, before backtracking to speak to a cashier.

Neither Clarkson nor Art of Play immediately replied to ABC News' request for comment.

articles.title: Ektaa Kapoor calls out alleged ‘Hinduphobia’ in the entertainment industry, questions why openly expressing religious identity is a problem: ‘Wearing your religion on your sleeve is such a problem’
articles.summary: Producer Ektaa Kapoor has opened up about the bias she believes exists in the entertainment industry towards Hindu culture and faith.
articles.body: Producer Ektaa Kapoor has opened up about the bias she believes exists in the entertainment industry towards Hindu culture and faith. She said she has been judged for openly practising her religion and wondered why Western traditions are easily accepted while Hindu customs are questioned.Ekta Kapoor on ‘Hinduphobia’ in the industrySpeaking with Ranveer Allahbadia on his podcast, Ektaa Kapoor said this prejudice becomes visible the moment Indian folklore, culture or faith comes into a story. She said, "Numbers are great for the film. What is really important is it deals with folklore. I’m just gonna say it on camera, Hinduphobia, and we have so much of phobia with what do we call... We’re okay with animated animation, but we’re not okay with discussing folklore and mythology."During the same conversation, the producer stated that she believes things are slowly changing for the better. "So I’m so okay with bringing it all out and having people accept it. There’s so much more acceptance now,” said the producer, who recently backed the mythological thriller ‘The Vvaan’.Ektaa Kapoor recalls being mocked for wearing a tika and dhaagaEktaa Kapoor also remembered how, in her younger days, people called her a freak and made fun of her for wearing a tika and dhaaga. She is known for wearing several rings, sacred threads and bracelets, and she spoke honestly about how hard it can be to show one’s religious identity in public. "I can’t even tell you. Wearing a tika and wearing your religion on your sleeve is such a problem," she said.Ektaa Kapoor recalled being judged for going to a club from a mandirThe producer also shared an incident when she was judged for heading to a club straight from a mandir. People around her were surprised and asked, “Did you go to a mandir?” She replied, “Yeah,” and then asked why the reaction was so shocking, saying, “What’s so shocking?”About ‘The Vvaan’The film stars Sidharth Malhotra and Tamannaah Bhatia. It mixes fantasy, folklore and supernatural elements and unfolds around a forbidden forest. articles.title: Santiago Segura alucina con el atraco frustrado a un establecimiento español: "Esto dentro de una película sería tachado de poco creíble o exagerado"
articles.standfirst: El vídeo de la cámara de seguridad ha sido publicado por La Vanguardia
articles.summary: El vídeo de la cámara de seguridad ha sido publicado por La Vanguardia
articles.body: Cuando se utiliza la expresión ‘la realidad supera a la ficción’ es porque algo extremadamente alucinante ha tenido que ocurrir. En redes sociales, se ha viralizado un vídeo publicado por La Vanguardia en el que una asaltante amenaza al dueño de un comercio con un cuchillo. Lo que parece un asalto armado acaba convirtiéndose en un atraco frustrado. La asaltante entra con un cuchillo en la mano y su única petición en todo el atraco es que se cierren las persianas. Su voz deja entrever que está un poco nerviosa, algo de lo que también parece darse cuenta el dependiente. Después de varios amagos, este se hace con una silla y se enfrenta desde detrás del mostrador a la ladrona. “Yo no te conozco a ti. Cierra la persiana o si no, hoy estás muerto. ¡Ciérrala ya!”, grita en varias ocasiones. Después, llegan las amenazas: “No me des con la silla que te clavo el cuchillo y te mato”. Mientras tanto, el dependiente intenta ahuyentarla con varios amagos con la silla sin mucho éxito. “Cierra la persiana. Te clavo el cuchillo y te mato”, insiste ella. “Tú me vas a hacer daño, pero yo te voy a matar”, sigue amenazando la ladrona. Sin embargo, en un momento dado, el dependiente se abalanza sobre ella y casi logra quitarle el arma. En ese instante, cuando se da cuenta de que su atraco no va a salir bien: “Mira, me voy porque me voy, porque me está entrando un ataque de ansiedad”. Esta escena ha dejado sin palabras, entre otros, a Santiago Segura. El director de ‘Torrente’ cree que estas imágenes no se acabarían de creer si ocurren en el cine: “Fascinantes escenas como esta demuestran cómo casi siempre la realidad supera a la ficción. (También te digo que esto dentro de una película sería tachado de poco creíble o exagerado)”.

articles.body:
Milan confirm that Strahinja Pavlović has signed a contract extension until June 2031.

Multiple Italian sources reported on Tuesday that Milan and Pavlović had reached an agreement on a new deal, and the club has now confirmed it.

Pavlovic extends Milan contract: official statement

MILAN, ITALY – AUGUST 28: Strahinja Pavlovic and Matteo Gabbia of AC Milan celebrate after the Serie A match between AC Milan and Venezia FC at Stadio Giuseppe Meazza on August 28, 2026 in Milan, Italy. (Photo by Marco Luzzani/Getty Images)

"AC Milan is pleased to announce that Strahinja Pavlović has signed a contract extension until 30 June 2031, with an option to extend," the Rossoneri said on Wednesday.

"Since joining the Rossoneri in July 2024, Strahinja has continued to grow, establishing himself as a point of reference through his professionalism, charisma and leadership, as well as the strong sense of belonging that distinguishes him both on and off the pitch.

GENOA, ITALY – MAY 17: Lorenzo Colombo of Genoa (left) and Strahinja Pavlovic of Milan vie for the ball during the Serie A match between Genoa CFC and AC Milan at Stadio Luigi Ferraris on May 17, 2026 in Genoa, Italy. (Photo by Simone Arveda/Getty Images)

"Pavlović has made 80 appearances for AC Milan, 75 of them as a starter, and scored 7 goals. This contract extension builds on the journey that began two years ago and lays the foundations for the future, reflecting the ambition to continue moving forward together and achieve new milestones."

Pavlovic, 25, joined Milan from RB Salzburg in 2024 for €18.5m.

He has provided one assist in seven appearances across all competitions this season.

articles.title: 'Jon & Kate Plus 8' star Collin Gosselin accuses mom of trying to 'bury' him to ‘protect her reputation’
articles.summary: Collin Gosselin alleges Kate Gosselin tried to "bury" him to protect her reputation, detailing childhood abuse claims and demanding accountability.
articles.body: Collin Gosselin is taking aim at his estranged mother, Kate Gosselin, accusing the former reality TV star of trying to "bury" him to protect her public image as he makes allegations of childhood abuse in his new memoir, "In the Shadow of Eight." In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, the "Jon & Kate Plus 8" alum said he has not spoken to Kate since he was 13 and would need an apology and accountability before considering reconciliation. "I'd like an apology, simply put, an apology and for her to admit, and just take accountability for what she did," Collin, 22, said. COLLIN GOSSELIN SENDS CRYPTIC SIGNAL TO MOM KATE AFTER CLAIMS SHE'S 'SPIRALING' OVER HIS UPCOMING MEMOIR "And to say, you know, 'I'm sorry that I've soiled your name, and I've made every effort to bury you, to protect my reputation,' I think that'd be very honest and very powerful for her to say that … just show accountability because everything she's done to protect her reputation, it's all been at my cost." In his memoir, "In the Shadow of Eight: Surviving the Reality of My Childhood," Collin alleged he endured physical abuse, isolation and forced psychiatric medication as a child. He also compared his experience in a treatment facility to being sent to a juvenile detention center, saying it left lasting scars. Collin said he held on to hope even during what he described as his darkest moments. KATE GOSSELIN CALLED A 'MONSTER' IN SOCIAL MEDIA COMMENTS AFTER SON COLLIN ANNOUNCES MEMOIR "I had very little hope, but I always had some, and I hung on to that … I just kept telling myself that there's a better future for me and there will be a time where I will be past this," he said. The former child star said sharing his story had weighed on him for years before he finally decided to speak publicly. WATCH: COLLIN GOSSELIN BLASTS MOM KATE FOR 'BURYING' HIM TO SAVE HER REPUTATION "It was heavy on my heart, my whole life, but especially now, it was just, I just felt like it was the time to do that," he said. The rift with Kate remains deep. Collin recalled a visit from his mother when he was 13, claiming the encounter left him with a painful final memory. "She berated me for all of 20 minutes after not seeing me for over a year," he said. KATE GOSSELIN DEFENDS HERSELF AGAINST SON COLLIN AS HE PREPARES TO RELEASE SHOCKING NEW MEMOIR Collin also described the effects of the psychiatric medication he said he was allegedly forced to take as a child, saying it left him feeling like a "zombie." In his memoir, he portrayed his childhood away from the cameras that made his family famous as deeply isolating. WATCH: COLLIN GOSSELIN DETAILS ALLEGED ABUSE, CONFRONTS FAMILY TRAUMA Despite the estrangement, Collin said he had not ruled out taking a call from Kate. But forgiveness, he stressed, would not automatically mean reconciliation. "Reconciliation requires action and accountability," he said. "I think we can all say, 'I'm sorry,' but if we're not willing to take the actions and take accountability for what has happened in the past and what happened my entire childhood, then what does that really mean, you know?" Collin said he remains open to hearing from his mother, hoping she might acknowledge what he alleges happened during his childhood.
